sectionTitle: Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations). Lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper compounds produce distinctive colours in flame tests:
lithium compounds result in a crimson flame
sodium compounds result in a yellow flame
potassium compounds result in a lilac flame
calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame
copper compounds result in a green flame.
If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used some flame colours can be masked.
Students should be able to identify species from the results of the tests in 4.8.3.1 to 4.8.3.5.
Flame colours of other metal ions are not required knowledge.
Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added but only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate.
Students should be able to write balanced equations for the reactions to produce the insoluble hydroxides.
Students are not expected to write equations for the production of sodium aluminate.
Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas. Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater.
Halide ions in solution produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid. Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.
Required practical 7: use of chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds covering the ions from sections Flame tests to Sulfates .
Elements and compounds can be detected and identified using instrumental methods. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
Students should be able to state advantages of instrumental methods compared with the chemical tests in this specification.
Flame emission spectroscopy is an example of an instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

The sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope. The output is a line spectrum that can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and measure their concentrations.

Students should be able to interpret an instrumental result given appropriate data in chart or tabular form, when accompanied by a reference set in the same form, limited to flame emission spectroscopy.

scopeNotes.statement: Flame colours of other metal ions are not required knowledge.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the five flame colours named in the specification are taught and tested here: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper green. No item asks for, or can be answered by, the flame colour of any other metal. The other metals that appear in this section (aluminium, magnesium, iron(II) and iron(III)) are identified only through their reactions with sodium hydroxide solution, and every option offered in a flame-test item is drawn from the five named colours.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write equations for the production of sodium aluminate.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Equation items are limited to the formation of the insoluble hydroxides, for example CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4 and FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4. The dissolving of aluminium hydroxide in excess sodium hydroxide solution is assessed only as an observation (the white precipitate redissolves); no item asks for, or offers as an option, an equation or formula for sodium aluminate.

concepts.definition: A test in which a sample of a compound is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame; some metal ions give the flame a distinctive colour, and that colour identifies the metal ion.
A positively charged ion. The metal ions identified by flame tests and by sodium hydroxide solution are cations.
The flame colour produced by lithium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by sodium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by potassium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by calcium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by copper compounds in a flame test.
When a sample contains a mixture of ions, one strong flame colour can hide, or mask, the colour produced by another metal ion, so that ion is not seen.

concepts.term: Identifying a species from test results
concepts.definition: Combining the results of the flame test, the sodium hydroxide test, the carbonate test, the halide test and the sulfate test to name the metal ion and the negative ion, and so the compound.
Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of an unknown salt; the colour of the metal hydroxide precipitate that forms identifies the metal ion.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed. In these tests the precipitate is a metal hydroxide, a silver halide or barium sulfate.
Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
Of the three white hydroxide precipitates, only aluminium hydroxide dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added; this distinguishes aluminium ions from calcium and magnesium ions.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured, not white, precipitates with sodium hydroxide solution.
The blue precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions.
Iron(II) ions give a green precipitate and iron(III) ions give a brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution.
A balanced symbol equation showing a metal salt solution reacting with sodium hydroxide solution to give the insoluble metal hydroxide, for example MgCl2 + 2NaOH -> Mg(OH)2 + 2NaCl.
Adding a dilute acid to the substance; carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas, seen as fizzing.
Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater: the gas is bubbled through limewater, which turns cloudy.
Adding dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution to the solution; halide ions produce a silver halide precipitate.
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution; sulfate ions produce a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
Using chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, covering the ions from the flame tests section through to the sulfates section.
A method of detecting and identifying elements and compounds using a machine rather than a chemical test. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
Compared with the chemical tests in this specification, instrumental methods are more accurate, more sensitive (they detect very small amounts) and faster.
An instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.
In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope; the output is a line spectrum.
A set of results for known substances, in the same chart or tabular form as the sample result, against which an instrumental result is compared to identify the ions present.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do sodium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium gives an orange flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium street lamps and burning sodium both look orange, and orange-red sits in the same list of colours for calcium.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is exact: sodium compounds result in a yellow flame. Orange-red belongs to calcium.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do lithium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Lithium gives an orange-red flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crimson and orange-red are both reds, and lithium and calcium are learned together as the two 'red' flame colours.
misconceptions.correction: Lithium is crimson; calcium is orange-red. The two must be kept apart.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do potassium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Potassium gives a blue flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lilac is an unfamiliar colour word, and students substitute a more familiar cool colour such as blue or purple.
misconceptions.correction: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame. No metal in this section gives a blue flame.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do calcium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Calcium gives a yellow flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Orange and yellow look similar in a Bunsen flame, and the sodium yellow is the colour students remember best.
misconceptions.correction: Calcium is orange-red; yellow belongs to sodium.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do copper compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Copper compounds result in a green flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper gives a blue flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue and copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate, so blue is strongly linked to copper.
misconceptions.correction: In a flame test copper compounds result in a green flame. Blue is the colour of the copper(II) hydroxide precipitate, not the flame.

misconceptions.question: What does a flame colour identify?
misconceptions.correct: The metal ion, the cation, in the compound.
misconceptions.misconception: The flame colour identifies the negative ion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compound names end with the negative ion, so students read the last word of the name as the thing being tested.
misconceptions.correction: Flame tests identify metal ions (cations). Negative ions are found with the carbonate, halide and sulfate tests.

misconceptions.question: What does a flame colour identify?
misconceptions.correct: The metal ion, the cation, in the compound.
misconceptions.misconception: The colour is a property of the whole compound, not of one ion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think in substances rather than ions, so 'copper sulfate burns green' feels like a fact about the compound.
misconceptions.correction: All copper compounds give the same green flame, whatever the negative ion, because the colour comes from the metal ion alone.

misconceptions.question: Why can one flame colour hide another?
misconceptions.correct: A strong colour can mask a weaker one in a mixture.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal that is not seen has been destroyed or has reacted away in the flame.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Not seeing something is read as it no longer being there, rather than as it being hidden.
misconceptions.correction: Both ions are still present. If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used, some flame colours can be masked.

misconceptions.question: What is seen when two metal ions are present?
misconceptions.correct: The stronger colour is seen; the other can be masked.
misconceptions.misconception: The two colours mix to give a completely new, third colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mixing paints or coloured lights gives a new colour, so the same is expected of flame colours.
misconceptions.correction: Flame colours are not mixed like paint; one intense colour simply hides the other.

misconceptions.question: Which ion does the sodium hydroxide test identify?
misconceptions.correct: It identifies the metal ion, the cation.
misconceptions.misconception: It identifies the negative ion in the salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A precipitate needs both ions, so students credit the wrong half of the salt with the result.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations); the precipitate is the metal hydroxide.

misconceptions.question: Which white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide?
misconceptions.misconception: All three white precipitates dissolve if enough sodium hydroxide is added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students generalise 'excess dissolves the precipitate' from the aluminium case to every white precipitate.
misconceptions.correction: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution; calcium and magnesium hydroxides stay.

misconceptions.question: Which white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide?
misconceptions.misconception: The calcium hydroxide precipitate is the one that dissolves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Calcium hydroxide is met as limewater, a solution, so students assume it is the soluble one.
misconceptions.correction: The precipitate that redissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution is aluminium hydroxide.

misconceptions.question: What is seen when sodium hydroxide is added to aluminium ions?
misconceptions.misconception: Aluminium ions give no precipitate at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Because the precipitate dissolves again in excess, students remember only the clear final solution.
misconceptions.correction: A white precipitate forms first; it dissolves only when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added.

misconceptions.question: Which ions give coloured precipitates with sodium hydroxide?
misconceptions.misconception: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium give the coloured precipitates.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two sets of three ions are learned as one list and are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium give white precipitates; copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) give coloured ones.

misconceptions.question: What colour precipitates do iron(II) and iron(III) give?
misconceptions.misconception: Iron(II) gives brown and iron(III) gives green.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two iron ions differ only by a Roman numeral, so the pairing of colour to charge is easily reversed.
misconceptions.correction: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate; iron(III) forms a brown precipitate.

misconceptions.question: What colour precipitate does copper(II) give?
misconceptions.misconception: Copper(II) gives a green precipitate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper is linked to green from the flame test and from green copper roofs, so green is carried across.
misconceptions.correction: Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution; the green flame is a separate result.

misconceptions.question: How many sodium hydroxides are needed per metal ion?
misconceptions.misconception: One sodium hydroxide is enough, as in CuSO4 + NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students copy the reactants across without counting atoms, and the equation looks tidy.
misconceptions.correction: A 2+ metal ion needs two hydroxide ions: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4 is the balanced equation.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of the hydroxide of iron(II)?
misconceptions.misconception: Iron always forms Fe(OH)3.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iron(III) compounds are met more often, so the 3+ charge is treated as iron's only charge.
misconceptions.correction: Iron(II) forms Fe(OH)2 and iron(III) forms Fe(OH)3; the Roman numeral gives the charge.

misconceptions.question: What gas do carbonates give with dilute acids?
misconceptions.misconception: Carbonates give off hydrogen with dilute acids.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acid plus metal gives hydrogen, and that far more common reaction is applied to carbonates too.
misconceptions.correction: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.

misconceptions.question: What gas do carbonates give with dilute acids?
misconceptions.misconception: Carbonates give off oxygen because the carbonate ion contains oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting the oxygen atoms in the formula is mistaken for predicting the product.
misconceptions.correction: The gas formed is carbon dioxide, identified because it turns limewater cloudy.

misconceptions.question: What does limewater do in a positive test?
misconceptions.misconception: Limewater turns blue when carbon dioxide is bubbled through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour-change indicators are the commonest test students meet, so a colour rather than a cloudiness is expected.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy; the cloudiness is solid calcium carbonate.

misconceptions.question: How is carbon dioxide identified?
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide relights a glowing splint.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The gas tests are learned as a set and the splint tests are swapped between gases.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide is identified with limewater, which turns cloudy.

misconceptions.question: What colour is silver chloride?
misconceptions.misconception: Silver chloride is cream and silver bromide is white.
misconceptions.whyItArises: White and cream are hard to tell apart, so the pairing with the halide is easily reversed.
misconceptions.correction: Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.

misconceptions.question: What colour is silver iodide?
misconceptions.misconception: Silver iodide is white, like the other silver halides.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iodine solution is brown, so no colour is firmly attached to iodide and white is used as a default.
misconceptions.correction: Silver iodide is yellow.

misconceptions.question: Which acid is used in the test for halide ions?
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used before adding silver nitrate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydrochloric acid is the acid used most often in the laboratory, and it is the acid used in the sulfate test.
misconceptions.correction: Halide ions produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid. Hydrochloric acid would add chloride ions of its own.

misconceptions.question: Which reagents test for sulfate ions?
misconceptions.correct: Dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution test for sulfates.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The halide test and the sulfate test both use an acid and then a solution, and both can give a white precipitate.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfate ions produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

misconceptions.question: What does a white precipitate with barium chloride show?
misconceptions.misconception: It shows chloride ions are present, because barium chloride was added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word chloride appears in the reagent's name, so it is read as the ion being detected.
misconceptions.correction: The reagent supplies barium ions; the white precipitate is barium sulfate, so sulfate ions are present.

misconceptions.question: How are instrumental methods described?
misconceptions.misconception: Instrumental methods are accurate but slow.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Machines in industry are pictured as needing long, careful runs, and accuracy is assumed to cost time.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

misconceptions.question: What is an advantage of an instrumental method?
misconceptions.correct: It detects very small amounts quickly and accurately.
misconceptions.misconception: An instrumental method works without needing a sample of the substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sensitive is read as needing no sample at all, rather than needing only a very small one.
misconceptions.correction: A sample is still needed; the advantage is that a very small sample is enough.

misconceptions.question: What does flame emission spectroscopy analyse?
misconceptions.misconception: It analyses non-metal ions, such as halides and sulfates.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students want a single instrument that replaces every chemical test in the section.
misconceptions.correction: Flame emission spectroscopy is used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

misconceptions.question: What is the light passed through?
misconceptions.correct: A spectroscope, giving a line spectrum.
misconceptions.misconception: The light is passed through a coloured filter to give a single colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Flame tests are judged by eye, so the instrument is imagined as a better way of seeing one colour.
misconceptions.correction: The light given out is passed through a spectroscope, and the output is a line spectrum.

misconceptions.question: What does a spectrum with two sets of lines show?
misconceptions.misconception: Only the ion with the brightest lines is present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Flame tests give one visible colour, so students expect one answer from a spectrum too.
misconceptions.correction: A line spectrum can show several metal ions at once; each set of lines matching a reference means that ion is present.

misconceptions.question: What does fizzing with dilute acid show?
misconceptions.misconception: Fizzing with dilute acid shows a sulfate is present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All the negative-ion tests are learned together, and any bubbling is treated as a general positive result.
misconceptions.correction: Only carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas; sulfates give a white precipitate with barium chloride.

misconceptions.question: What else can a line spectrum give?
misconceptions.correct: The concentration of the metal ions.
misconceptions.misconception: A line spectrum can only say which ions are present, never how much.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Identification is the obvious use, so the quantitative use is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: The line spectrum can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and to measure their concentrations.

misconceptions.question: How is an unknown single ionic compound identified?
misconceptions.correct: One test for the metal ion and one for the negative ion.
misconceptions.misconception: A flame test on its own is enough to name the compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The flame test is quick and gives a clear result, so it feels like a complete identification.
misconceptions.correction: The flame test names only the metal ion; a second test is needed for the negative ion before the compound can be named.

misconceptions.question: Are instrumental methods cheaper than chemical tests?
misconceptions.correct: No; the instrument is expensive to buy and to run.
misconceptions.misconception: An instrumental method must be cheaper because a machine does the work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Automatic is equated with cheap, and the cost of buying and maintaining the instrument is invisible to a student.
misconceptions.correction: The advantages stated are accuracy, sensitivity and speed. Instruments are costly, so a simple chemical test can be the cheaper option.

mcqs.stem: A student holds a small sample of an unknown ionic compound on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame, and a strong colour appears. What does the flame colour identify?

options.text: the metal ion, the cation, present in that compound
options.rationale: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

options.text: the negative ion, the anion, in the compound
options.rationale: The compound's name ends with the negative ion, so students test the last word they read.

options.text: the compound as a whole and not one of its ions
options.rationale: Thinking in substances rather than ions makes the colour a property of the compound.

options.text: the temperature reached by the Bunsen flame
options.rationale: Flame colour is linked to heat in everyday life, so temperature is a tempting reading.

mcqs.stem: Lithium chloride is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame. What is seen?

options.text: The flame turns a bright yellow colour.
options.rationale: Yellow is the flame colour students recall first, and it belongs to sodium.

options.text: The flame turns a deep crimson colour.
options.rationale: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.

options.text: The flame turns an orange-red colour.
options.rationale: Crimson and orange-red are both reds, so lithium and calcium are swapped.

options.text: The flame turns a pale lilac colour.
options.rationale: Lilac is the potassium colour, offered here because lithium and potassium are both group 1.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride is used in a flame test. Which statement describes the result?

options.text: Sodium ions colour the flame bright orange.
options.rationale: Sodium street lamps glow orange, so orange feels like the sodium colour.

options.text: Sodium ions colour the flame crimson red.
options.rationale: Crimson is the lithium colour; the two group 1 metals are confused.

options.text: Sodium ions colour the flame yellow.
options.rationale: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.

options.text: Sodium ions colour the flame lilac.
options.rationale: Lilac belongs to potassium, the other common group 1 metal in this test.

mcqs.stem: Potassium bromide is tested in a flame test. What is the result?

options.text: The flame colour produced is yellow.
options.rationale: Yellow is the most memorable flame colour, but it belongs to sodium.

options.text: The flame colour produced is crimson.
options.rationale: An unfamiliar colour word is replaced by a familiar one from the same list.

options.text: The flame colour produced is orange-red.
options.rationale: Orange-red is the calcium colour, offered because both metals are common salts.

options.text: The flame colour produced is lilac.
options.rationale: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.

mcqs.stem: Calcium nitrate gives a distinctive colour in a flame test. Which colour is it?

options.text: a pale green flame colour
options.rationale: Green is the copper colour, offered because both are common laboratory salts.

options.text: an orange-red flame colour
options.rationale: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.

options.text: a bright crimson colour
options.rationale: Crimson belongs to lithium; both are reds and are easily swapped.

options.text: a bright yellow colour
options.rationale: Orange and yellow look similar in a flame, and yellow is the sodium colour.

mcqs.stem: Copper(II) sulfate is held in a hot Bunsen flame during a flame test. What is seen?

options.text: The flame is coloured a crimson red.
options.rationale: Crimson is the lithium colour, offered as a distinctive alternative.

options.text: The flame is coloured pale blue.
options.rationale: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, so blue is strongly linked to copper.

options.text: The flame is coloured a bright green.
options.rationale: Copper compounds result in a green flame.

options.text: The flame colour does not change at all.
options.rationale: Students who think only group 1 and 2 metals give colours expect no change.

mcqs.stem: A solution contains both sodium ions and potassium ions. In a flame test only a yellow colour is seen. Why is the lilac colour of potassium not seen?

options.text: The potassium ions are destroyed in the flame.
options.rationale: Not seeing the colour is read as the ion no longer being there.

options.text: The two colours mix to give a new colour.
options.rationale: Mixing paints gives a new colour, so the same is expected of flames.

options.text: Potassium needs a hotter flame than this one.
options.rationale: A missing result is blamed on the apparatus rather than on masking.

options.text: The intense sodium colour masks the lilac.
options.rationale: If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used some flame colours can be masked.

mcqs.stem: An unknown compound gives a yellow flame test colour. Its solution gives a white precipitate when dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution are added. What is the compound?

options.text: sodium sulfate
options.rationale: The yellow flame shows sodium ions and the white precipitate with acidified barium chloride shows sulfate ions.

options.text: potassium sulfate
options.rationale: The correct negative ion is chosen but the flame colour is read as potassium.

options.text: sodium carbonate
options.rationale: Any positive result with a dilute acid is treated as showing a carbonate.

options.text: sodium chloride
options.rationale: The white precipitate is credited to chloride, confusing this test with the halide test.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown salt and a precipitate forms. Which ion in the salt does this test identify?

options.text: the negative ion in the salt, its anion
options.rationale: A precipitate needs both ions, so the wrong half of the salt is credited.

options.text: the sodium ion in the sodium hydroxide
options.rationale: The reagent's own metal ion is mistaken for the ion being identified.

options.text: the positive metal ion in the salt, its cation
options.rationale: Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

options.text: both of the ions in the salt at one time
options.rationale: One test is assumed to give a complete identification of the compound.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added, a few drops at a time, to separate solutions of aluminium ions, calcium ions and magnesium ions. What is seen in each tube?

options.text: A white precipitate forms in two of the tubes.
options.rationale: The aluminium precipitate is forgotten because it later redissolves.

options.text: A coloured precipitate forms in each tube.
options.rationale: The two sets of three metal ions are swapped over.

options.text: A white precipitate forms in one tube only.
options.rationale: Only the most familiar of the three metals is expected to react.

options.text: A white precipitate forms in all three tubes.
options.rationale: Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

mcqs.stem: Excess sodium hydroxide solution is now added to the three white precipitates formed from aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions. What happens?

options.text: Only the aluminium hydroxide dissolves.
options.rationale: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

options.text: Only the calcium hydroxide dissolves.
options.rationale: Calcium hydroxide is met as limewater, a solution, so it is assumed to be soluble.

options.text: All three of the white hydroxides dissolve.
options.rationale: The aluminium result is generalised to every white precipitate.

options.text: None of the three precipitates dissolves.
options.rationale: Precipitates are treated as permanently insoluble once formed.

mcqs.stem: Which set of metal ions all give coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added to their solutions?

options.text: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions
options.rationale: The white-precipitate set and the coloured-precipitate set are swapped.

options.text: copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III)
options.rationale: Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

options.text: copper(II), calcium and magnesium ions
options.rationale: One coloured ion is kept and the rest of the white set is added to it.

options.text: iron(II), iron(III) and the aluminium ion
options.rationale: Aluminium is grouped with the irons because all three are common metals.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution. What is seen?

options.text: a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide
options.rationale: The colours of the two iron ions are reversed.

options.text: a blue precipitate of copper hydroxide
options.rationale: Blue is attached to the wrong metal ion.

options.text: a white precipitate that then dissolves
options.rationale: The aluminium behaviour is applied to iron.

options.text: a brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide
options.rationale: Iron(III) forms a brown precipitate.

mcqs.stem: A solution gives a green precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion does the solution contain?

options.text: The solution contains iron(II) ions.
options.rationale: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate.

options.text: The solution contains copper(II) ions.
options.rationale: Copper is linked with green from its flame colour, not from its precipitate.

options.text: It is a solution of iron(III) ions.
options.rationale: The green and brown precipitates of the two iron ions are swapped.

options.text: It is a magnesium salt in water.
options.rationale: Magnesium gives a white precipitate, but it is a common ion in these tests.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and a blue precipitate forms. Which equation for this reaction is correct and balanced?

options.text: CuSO4 + NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: Reactants are copied across without counting atoms.

options.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: Two hydroxide ions are needed for each Cu2+ ion, and every atom balances.

options.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + 2Na2SO4
options.rationale: The sodium is not counted, so the sulfate is wrongly doubled.

options.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> CuOH + Na2SO4 + H2
options.rationale: Hydrogen gas is invented because an acid-like reaction is expected.

mcqs.stem: Iron(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give a green precipitate. Which equation is correct and balanced?

options.text: Fe2SO4 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: Iron is assumed always to form the 3+ hydroxide.

options.text: 2FeSO4 + 4NaOH -> 2Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: The formulae are doubled without checking the sulfur atoms.

options.text: FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: Iron(II) is Fe2+, so the insoluble hydroxide is Fe(OH)2 and two NaOH are needed.

options.text: FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4 + H2
options.rationale: Hydrogen gas is invented because an acid-like reaction is expected.

mcqs.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a white solid that is thought to be a carbonate. What is seen, and what gas is given off?

options.text: It fizzes, giving off carbon dioxide gas.
options.rationale: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.

options.text: It fizzes, giving off hydrogen gas.
options.rationale: Acid plus metal gives hydrogen, and that reaction is applied here.

options.text: It fizzes, giving off oxygen gas.
options.rationale: The oxygen atoms in the carbonate formula are read as the product.

options.text: It dissolves quietly, giving off no gas.
options.rationale: Dissolving is confused with reacting.

mcqs.stem: The gas given off when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid is bubbled through limewater. What is the positive result?

options.text: The limewater relights a glowing splint.
options.rationale: The gas tests are learned together and the splint tests are swapped.

options.text: The limewater turns cloudy, or milky.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater, which turns cloudy.

options.text: The limewater turns a bright blue.
options.rationale: A colour change is expected because indicators are the commonest test.

options.text: The limewater becomes colourless.
options.rationale: Limewater is colourless already, but decolourising is a familiar phrase.

mcqs.stem: Dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added to a solution of an unknown halide. A cream precipitate forms. What does the solution contain?

options.text: The unknown solution contains chloride ions.
options.rationale: White and cream are hard to tell apart, so the two are swapped.

options.text: The unknown solution contains carbonate ions.
options.rationale: Any precipitate is treated as a general positive result.

options.text: The unknown solution contains bromide ions.
options.rationale: Silver bromide is cream.

options.text: The unknown solution contains iodide ions.
options.rationale: No firm colour is attached to iodide, so it is guessed.

mcqs.stem: A solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution is added. A yellow precipitate forms. Which ion is present?

options.text: the bromide ion, Br-
options.rationale: Cream and yellow are close in appearance, so bromide is chosen.

options.text: the chloride ion, Cl-
options.rationale: White is treated as the default colour for every silver halide.

options.text: the sulfate ion, SO4 2-
options.rationale: The halide test and the sulfate test are confused.

options.text: the iodide ion, I-
options.rationale: Silver iodide is yellow.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to show that a solution contains sulfate ions. What should be added, and what is a positive result?

options.text: dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate
options.rationale: The halide test is used because it also gives a white precipitate.

options.text: dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate
options.rationale: Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

options.text: dilute hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide: a white precipitate
options.rationale: The cation test is used to look for a negative ion.

options.text: barium chloride solution alone: a cream coloured precipitate
options.rationale: The acid step is omitted and the wrong colour is recalled.

mcqs.stem: Barium chloride solution is added to a solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid, and a white precipitate forms. What does this show?

options.text: Chloride ions are present in this solution.
options.rationale: The word chloride in the reagent's name is read as the ion detected.

options.text: Carbonate ions are present in solution.
options.rationale: Any positive result with an acid present is credited to a carbonate.

options.text: Sulfate ions are present in the solution.
options.rationale: The white precipitate is barium sulfate, so sulfate ions are present.

options.text: Barium ions are present in solution.
options.rationale: The reagent's own metal ion is treated as the unknown.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 7 a student is given a solution of a single unknown ionic compound and must name it. Which plan will identify the compound?

options.text: adding sodium hydroxide, then silver nitrate
options.rationale: Only cation reagents are chosen, so no halide result is obtained.

options.text: adding barium chloride solution on its own
options.rationale: A single negative-ion test is treated as naming the compound.

options.text: just a flame test on its own is enough
options.rationale: The flame test gives a clear result, so it feels like a full identification.

options.text: a flame test, then a test for the anion
options.rationale: The compound is named only when both its metal ion and its negative ion have been identified.

mcqs.stem: The specification describes instrumental methods of analysis. Which three words does it use?

options.text: accurate, sensitive and rapid
options.rationale: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

options.text: accurate and sensitive, but slow
options.rationale: Careful machine analysis is assumed to take a long time.

options.text: cheap, simple and easy to carry
options.rationale: Instruments are assumed to be simple because they are automatic.

options.text: rapid, but not really accurate
options.rationale: Speed is assumed to be traded against accuracy.

mcqs.stem: Give one advantage of using an instrumental method instead of the chemical tests in this specification.

options.text: It can be used without taking a sample at all.
options.rationale: Sensitive is read as needing no sample rather than a small one.

options.text: It gives a result that never needs any checking.
options.rationale: Machine results are treated as beyond question.

options.text: It can detect a very small amount of a substance quickly.
options.rationale: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

options.text: It is always cheaper than a simple chemical test.
options.rationale: Automatic is assumed to mean low cost.

mcqs.stem: Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method. What is it used to analyse?

options.text: the non-metal ions present in solids
options.rationale: One instrument is expected to replace every chemical test.

options.text: the gases given off by a solution
options.rationale: Instrumental analysis is confused with testing for gases.

options.text: the mass of a solid sample taken
options.rationale: Any laboratory instrument is assumed to weigh things.

options.text: the metal ions present in solutions
options.rationale: Flame emission spectroscopy is used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

mcqs.stem: In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame. What happens to the light given out, and what is the output?

options.text: It passes into a spectroscope, giving a line spectrum.
options.rationale: The light given out is passed through a spectroscope and the output is a line spectrum.

options.text: It is absorbed by the sample, giving a set of dark bands.
options.rationale: Absorption spectra are confused with emission spectra.

options.text: It passes through a coloured filter, giving one colour.
options.rationale: The instrument is imagined as a better way of seeing a flame colour.

options.text: It warms a sensor, giving a temperature reading.
options.rationale: A flame instrument is assumed to measure heat.

mcqs.stem: A student is given the line spectrum of a solution together with a reference set of line spectra for known metal ions. The sample spectrum contains every line of the lithium reference and every line of the calcium reference. What should the student conclude?

options.text: Only the ion with the brighter lines is present.
options.rationale: One visible flame colour leads students to expect one answer.

options.text: Lithium ions and calcium ions are both present.
options.rationale: Each set of reference lines that appears in the sample spectrum shows that metal ion is present.

options.text: A new metal ion not in the reference set is there.
options.rationale: Two overlapping sets of lines are read as one unknown substance.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded from a spectrum like this.
options.rationale: Mixtures are assumed to make an instrumental result useless.
